exhibits.title: The Unnamed Form
exhibits.text:
On the plinth stands a shape no sculptor set out to carve. Walk around it: from one side it is unmistakably a BIRD'S WING, elongated, planar, feathered at the trailing edge. From the other it is a PLANE'S WING, the same long silhouette, the same aerodynamic set, riveted metal where the feathers were. It is one form holding both, and no hand ever named it 'wing'.

That is the wonder this gallery exists to explain. The self-supervised eye of the room before this one was never told what a wing is, never given the word, never shown a labelled example. Yet probe its features and bird wings and plane wings land in nearly the same place, recognised as kin. The concept was not taught. It EMERGED, as an unavoidable consequence of the objective.

Recall the demand: a student, shown only a small local crop, must predict what the teacher sees of the whole. Show it a crop that is just a wing, and to succeed it must encode something that PREDICTS the global scene, 'elongated, attached to a body, aerodynamic, belongs against sky, part of a flying thing'. A bird's wing and a plane's wing must predict almost the same whole. So the most efficient way to encode them is TOGETHER. The gallery is full of such unnamed forms, each one a code the network invented because inventing it was cheaper than not.

exhibits.title: The Concept No One Named
exhibits.text:
Nothing ever told the self-supervised eye what a wing is. No label, no caption, no example marked 'wing'. And yet the concept is there in the features, bird wings and plane wings sitting close together as a shared idea.

The mechanism is the local-to-global objective itself. The student sees a LOCAL crop, perhaps just a wing, and must predict what the TEACHER sees looking at the WHOLE image. So the wing-patch representation is forced to carry whatever predicts its global context: elongated and planar, attached to a central body, an aerodynamic silhouette, appearing in scenes of sky and flight.

The concept is not a category the network was handed. It is a by-product. A reusable pattern the objective made it worth discovering. You learn what a wing is not because anyone said so, but because encoding wings well is the only way to predict the wholes they belong to.

exhibits.title: Why Bird and Plane Converge
exhibits.text:
Why should a feathered wing and a metal one end up near each other, with nothing linking them but geometry?

Because they share what the objective cares about. Both are elongated planar shapes. Both attach to a central body. Both cast a similar silhouette, and both co-occur with sky and flight. And so both must PREDICT SIMILAR GLOBAL CONTEXTS, a flying thing set against open air.

When two visual parts must predict the same kind of whole, the most efficient encoding groups them together. Keeping a bird-wing code and a plane-wing code strictly apart would cost the network capacity and buy it nothing, since they behave identically under the objective. So they converge to nearby representations, not because they are 'both wings' in any dictionary sense, but because they play the same role in the same kinds of scenes.

exhibits.title: Compression Is the Sculptor
exhibits.text:
The deeper principle: the network has LIMITED CAPACITY and must compress. Abstraction is what falls out of that pressure.

A finite representation cannot afford a separate code for every appearance of every thing. The most efficient compression gives THE SAME CODE to things that behave the same way under the objective, visual parts that look alike, occur in similar contexts, and predict similar wholes. Keeping them separate would waste capacity for no gain; merging them is simply cheaper.

So abstraction here is not supervision in disguise. The model is not learning 'wing' as a labelled category. It is discovering that a certain visual-structural pattern is a useful, reusable unit, and that unit happens to line up with what we call a wing. This is why the attention maps are so striking: object structure appears with no segmentation labels because the visual world has enough statistical regularity that 'parts' are discoverable from co-occurrence and context alone. Abstraction emerges from compression pressure, not from being told.

exhibits.title: An Honest Warning
exhibits.text:
Do not leave this gallery believing the emergent concepts are guaranteed to be OUR concepts. They are not.

Emergent concepts align with human categories only WHERE VISUAL STATISTICS HAPPEN TO MATCH human semantics, often, but not always. The network groups by what predicts context under its objective; where that grouping coincides with a word we use, we get a pleasing 'wing'. Where it does not, the network's concept simply has no name in any language, and cuts the world along a seam we never drew.

And nothing NAMES them. The model never announces 'I have learned wing'. You only discover a concept exists by PROBING the features, measuring what sits near what. The gallery is full of unnamed forms precisely because that is their true condition: real, reusable, and mute.

exhibits.title: Two Wings, One Neighbourhood
exhibits.caption: A bird-wing crop and a plane-wing crop, mapped into the self-supervised feature space, land as near neighbours. The annotation traces why: both are elongated planar parts attached to a central body, both co-occur with sky and flight, and so both must predict nearly the same global context. Under COMPRESSION PRESSURE, a finite representation that cannot afford a separate code for every appearance, the cheapest encoding merges them into one shared code. That shared code is the emergent concept we happen to call 'wing'. It was learned from context prediction and capacity limits, never from a label.

exhibits.title: Of Concepts That Name Themselves
exhibits.text:
HOW 'WING' EMERGES WITHOUT LABELS

The DINOv2 paper showed something quietly astonishing: bird wings and plane wings recognised as similar semantic concepts, though nothing ever told the model what a wing is. The concept emerges as a consequence of the objective.

THE MECHANISM. The student sees a local crop, perhaps just a wing, and must predict what the teacher sees of the whole image. So the wing-patch representation must encode something that predicts global context: elongated, attached to a body, aerodynamic in shape, appearing in flying-object scenes.

WHY BIRD AND PLANE CONVERGE. Both share an elongated planar shape, attachment to a central body, a similar silhouette, and similar co-occurrence with sky and flight. Both must therefore predict similar global contexts, a flying thing against sky. The most efficient encoding groups them together, so they converge to nearby representations.

THE DEEPER PRINCIPLE. The network has limited capacity and must compress. The most efficient compression groups things that behave similarly under the objective. Visual parts that look alike, appear in similar contexts, and predict similar wholes get the SAME CODE, keeping them separate would waste capacity for no gain. That is abstraction emerging from compression pressure, not from supervision. The model is not learning 'wing' as a labelled category; it learns that a visual-structural pattern is a useful reusable unit, which happens to correspond to what we call a wing.

Why the attention maps are striking: object structure falls out of the representation with no segmentation labels. The visual world has enough statistical structure that 'parts' are discoverable purely from co-occurrence and context prediction.

AN HONEST CAVEAT. Emergent concepts are not guaranteed to align with human categories. They align where visual statistics happen to match human semantics, often, but not always. And nothing names them; you only discover a concept exists by probing the features.
